utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation] ... [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, as well as and all the people assisting the OTP. I would also like to greet Mr. Seselj and all the people present in helping us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will check.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a problem with the headphones. Sometimes I hear the interpretation into Serbian, sometimes into English. There's seems to be a mix-up with the channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we'll check. Mr. Seselj, can you hear the translation properly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do now. Yes, I do. Well, actually, I heard it a little while ago too, but then the Serbian would stop and then I would hear English, as if somebody was switching channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be working now. We shall resume cross-examination. I was saying that Mr. Seselj should still have an hour and a half. We shall bring the witness in the courtroom. I shall ask the usher to go and fetch him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I hope you had a nice evening. As you know, your cross-examination is going to resume now. Questions will be put to you by Mr. Seselj. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Baricevic, yesterday you spoke about a bus full of White Eagles who allegedly arrived before the rally in Hrtkovci from Sabac. And then you said that they had rifles, is that so? Which means automatic rifles, that's what it usually means. Is that what you meant? And you said that they wore all kinds of clothes and footwear, is that so? That means that nobody had a full uniform, a part of this uniform or part of that uniform, did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that a bus full of people, armed people had arrived, and parked in Savska Street, and that they had gone to the place where the rally was to be held, and that they were not dressed like military personnel, but in all kinds of clothes. And that they had automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, this is what I'm interested in, this diversity of their clothes. Did they wear different kinds of military clothing or civilian clothes? Did they wear different kinds of military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only difference was, in fact, in the boots they wore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they all have the same uniforms but different boots?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some had boots, some had shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that the only difference?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you can see that in any barracks; some soldiers wear boots, some wear shoes. What is so strange about it then? What was the diversity in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I answered you. I said that some had boots, others had shoes, but I just compared them with the regular army. I said that everybody has the same kinds of clothes and footwear.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fine. Let's leave the boots and shoes aside. You said that they had different kinds of uniforms, let's now focus on that. Were those camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kinds of uniforms there?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Black uniforms. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All of them wore black uniforms?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when was there ever a formation in Serbia wearing black uniforms? How come that nobody ever noticed that, ever?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, they came there dressed in the kind of clothes that I just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what party in Serbia set up the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what party founded the White Eagles, but that's how those people were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they said that they were White Eagles and Seselj's security; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did they attend the rally carrying those automatic rifles?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were mingling with the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, is there a single rally in Serbia that was attended by 50 people with automatic rifles? Did this happen at all anywhere, ever?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if there were any other rallies elsewhere, but I didn't say there were 50 of them. I just said that there was this bus that came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, usually you can fit about 50 people on the bus. Maybe the bus was half full, maybe there were just 30 people there, but you would not use a bus to bring just five or six people there, would you? Why would there be a bus if there wasn't a larger number of them? Those people who suggested to you that you should make this kind of statement did not really proof you all that well, they did not really teach you what to say, Mr. Baricevic, did they?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the number but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, witness. The Prosecutor is on his feet, but I know what he is going to -- I know what he's about to say. What do you want to say, Mr. Mussemeyer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to say that Mr. Seselj should refrain from these allegations that we are putting something in the witness mouth. He knows exactly that we proofed the witness, that we go through his former statement, that we constantly tell him that he has to tell the truth, and it is nothing from the side of the Prosecution to influence the witness, and Mr. Seselj knows this and he should refrain from this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you heard Mr. Seselj hint at the fact that somebody implied that you should say that. Did you say it or did somebody imply that you should say that? You understand my question? Let me repeat. A few moments ago you talked about those men who were armed, who were dressed in black, who were wearing shoes or boots and who attended Mr. Seselj's speech, which Mr. Seselj challenges. At one point he says that it was hinted that you should say that, and the Prosecutor has just got on his feet to say that they never hinted at anything. So my question is, did you say that or did somebody suggest that you should say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's check. Let me repeat. Can you hear the translation? I'll start from the beginning. You said that there were 30 or 50 people that were armed, dressed in black, wearing boots or shoes. Those people were present when Mr. Seselj delivered his speech, which Mr. Seselj challenges. And he said so. At one point, Mr. Seselj says that what you are saying is something that has been suggested to you. The Prosecutor got on his feet to say that they have never suggested anything whatsoever. This is my question: When you say this, does this come from you or did somebody ask you to say this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday that the bus had been parked in the Savska Street somewhere around number 7 and my house is at number 19, so that was in my street. I saw this bus there. Nobody told me to provide this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this time I did not accuse the Prosecution at all, and Mr. Mussemeyer, I think, responds because of his bad conscience, not because I levelled any accusations. But I would like to stress that we had some witnesses, Croats, in this trial and in some other trials, and it turned out that the Croatian intelligence service had prepped them before they came here to testify. There is documentary evidence to that effect. I brought some documents here to show that. So my question is completely regular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday Mr. Seselj put the question to you, but I shall put the question to you now. Did the Croatian intelligence services try to contact you with a view to making statements before this Tribunal, or did you never meet the Croatian intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday that I received a visit and they only asked me about these events that I was involved in. No record was made and nobody tried to talk me into anything when I gave the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember you saying that yesterday. But these two people who came, I believe there were two, why did they come? Was it to say hello to you and everything is all fine and well? Why did they come and see you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They asked me if I was able to find my way around there and they asked me how I was able to get from Hrtkovci to Jaksic. It was just a very brief conversation with them. They asked me more questions about my private life and how I intend to go on to fix the house, to do some farm work, what I should do to improve my situation as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two people who came, did they say that they worked for the Croatian Ministry of the Interior, did they show you an ID card? What did they actually tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They told me that they were from the military prosecutor's office in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the military prosecutor's office in Osijek, that's what they told you. And the military Prosecutor from Osijek is in charge of rebuilding your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. They asked me about the situation, and then we moved on and we had a private conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How far is it from Slavonska Pozega to Osijek in kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Not more than that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And they went all the way from Osijek to Slavonska Pozega to talk to you about your trip from Hrtkovci to Slavonska Pozega and what is the situation with the farm work?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we talked about farm work later, subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: At any rate, you travelled to Croatia via Hungary because that was the only way to do it. You went from Hrtkovci to Novi Sad to Subotica and then to Hungary; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did they ask you about, what could be of any interest to any military organs or military intelligence organs? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what they asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You know Slavko Kulundzic, do you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Ruma?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: From Ruma. He was in the state security?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You've known him for years?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How long? Since when?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992 or rather, well, maybe some five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Have you known him from before?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you were his informant in Hrtkovci, were you not?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was nobody's informant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, he says that you were. Slavko Kulundzic said that when he spoke to my expert team there, to assist my Defence, Nebojsa Sarevic and Jelena Bozetalijin [phoen]. And let me read what he had to say about you, and for the Prosecution that's at page 384 of my book. I've provided the book quite some time ago. He talked about some specific things that we will go back to but my associates say this: So you cooperated, the intelligence state security service cooperated with them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. The Prosecutor is raising an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Seselj is quoting from statements which we don't know, he should get used to deliver these statements to the Prosecution in advance and not surprise everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, from what I understood, but I stand to be corrected, I believe that the statement by this person named Slavko Kulundzic is part of a book which you published.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Prosecution knows about this book. It's on the basis of this book that they announced a criminal complaint against me and against my associates and they are going to charge us with contempt of court, and now they don't know about it. 15 or 20 days ago through the members of the registry, I handed it over to the OTP myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give us the title of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that if I give you the title, you are going to delete it or you are going to move into closed session. You know what heading it is, (redacted), and you know what follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... with pleasure utter the entire title, but I don't want us to move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This Slavko Kulundzic, what did he tell you that is contained in the book? Since the Prosecutor has a book, he can check straightaway. Mr. Mussemeyer, do you have this book and it's contained in the book?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Ms. Dahl informed me that we have this book. It's 1200 pages long. It's all in B/C/S and nobody in the Prosecution is able to translate this within 14 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The book hasn't been translated. Mr. Seselj, do not read out the entire book, just tell us what this man Slavko Kulundzic has said.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if the book has not been translated, how could they charge me with contempt of court? That is to say, that that someone told them about the book, and on the basis of that, they filed their complaint. This book was published more than a year ago, and since they prepared the complaint, after that they must have read the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, there have been select translations of particular witness statements, but I don't believe that it is fair play to a surprise the Prosecution with a selection from the 1200-page book. That is out of order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Mrs. Dahl. If I understand correctly, Mr. Seselj, based on this book, you have filed a motion, so you must have selected those pages you were interested in. It might have been a better idea to read the entire book since this book is not part of the trial and Mr. Seselj can say that someone has said such and such and the witness will answer by saying, I challenge this or I don't. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we need to discuss the book in private session to give me a fair chance to respond to what Mr. Seselj is saying and the observations that you have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, we shall move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Baricevic, Slavko Kulundzic is very explicit and he claims that for several years you collaborated with the state security service and that he was your contact, and that you regularly informed him about the situation in the village, what was going on, what people were saying and everything else. That is a claim made by Slavko Kulundzic.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, yesterday I stated that I and Dobrosav Markovic went to Ruma to the MUP to ask for help for the village, to have Slavko Kulundzic help us. Had I been his informant, he would have saved me and Dobrosav at least. Dobrosav and I both had to move out of the village. That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In relation to your trip to Ruma, he does confirm that you came, but that you came on private business to the SUP and then you dropped in to see him, as you did before. You chatted with him, had a cup of coffee and you did not complain about anything specific. You didn't say that you had any problems and you didn't ask him for any help. You came to take care of some business at the SUP, perhaps you were getting a passport or something like that, as people do at the SUP, and then you stopped to see him, as if he was an old friend basically. That is his version. I don't know him and I saw you for the first time yesterday, so I'm comparing your assertions to Slavko Kulundzic's assertions. Judges, in relation to this, I would have a separate statement signed and verified by Slavko Kulundzic had all my contacts not been severed with my associates; that is why I'm compelled to use the book. I have some other documents from the book that, otherwise, my associates would have sent me as original documents. Since I have no communications with them, I can only use the book. Isn't that right, Mr. Baricevic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that is the assertion he makes.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made my statement in 1992, before your book was written, and I did not know that Slavko would make that kind of statement. I gave the kind of statement as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who did you give this statement to in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Just shortly for the record, Mr. Seselj has the possibility to contact his associates. He is only not using it. He has repeated this several times and it should be corrected for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, please, sir, answer the question. Mr. Seselj put to you a question and your answer, again was I was not an informant for this person. So now proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slavko Kulundzic claims here, because he, himself, attended the rally, and he says that there were lots of policemen at the rally. He claims that no bus had come from Sabac with the White Eagles and he says that there were no White Eagles in black uniforms there at all. He also claims that no one attended the rally with weapons. Now, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I say is that that is not true. It is not true. It's not true that I was an informant and this is not true either. I can say exactly where the bus had been parked and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: We are not interested in where the bus was parked, we are interested in whether a group of White Eagles arrived in black uniforms to provide security for me or not. That's what I'm interested in. Who knows who had parked some bus there even a week before? I'm not interested in that. However, as for a bus from Sabac with a group of White Eagles in black uniforms, Slavko Kulundzic said that no one like that arrived, and he says if that had been the case, the police would have taken appropriate measures. It is impossible for that kind of thing to happen unobserved.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bus was in Savska Street, in front of number 7. These people got out of the bus, the ones that I've been talking about all of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Slavko Kulundzic says further on that I did not read out any list at that rally. What do you say that to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavko Kulundzic can claim whatever he wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Slavko Kulundzic informed his superiors ex officio about developments at the rally, not then and not now did he hear me reading out any list. Do you think that Slavko Kulundzic is lying for some reason?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, why then did he say to me to Ruma [as interpreted], whoever has to go should go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Slavko Kulundzic never said that to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move to private session for a few moments, Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session now, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Slavko Kulundzic claims that you did not complain to him at all. He also says that you did not announce that you would be leaving Hrtkovci. He believes that there was no reason for that, you never mentioned any pressures exerted against you or your family to him. He says that you never said that you had been mistreated. He also says that after so many years of collaboration, you had built a personal, friendly relationship and that once you even fixed the water pipes in his house. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what Slavko says, that I did not ask for help, that is not true. And that I went to fix one water pipe for him, well, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says that he was very satisfied with your cooperation, and that on the basis of that, sometimes he would help you when something was needed. He did not specify what that something was, truth to tell. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not give me any help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. That's what he says. All right. Let us not dwell on this any longer, what it is that Slavko Kulundzic says, because his statement is very, very interesting and I hope that he will show up here as a Defence witness, if there is a Defence case at all. You claimed that at the rally I read out a list. Is there a single person in Serbia who saw me reading anything at a public rally? Am I not well known throughout Serbia as a politician who speaks directly, who speaks off the cuff, except in the assembly when I'm criticizing a particular bill and when I have to read something out. Did you see that on television?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People heard who it was that had to move out, and now whether that was read out or whether it was just uttered, it came from your mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: People heard that others had already left Hrtkovci and registered with the ZNG, Tudjman's paramilitary units. This is what Zilic said. After that no names were read out. In my speech, there were no names of local persons. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did Aleksa Ejic found the Serb Radical Party in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said he did not, did we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you said that he did but I'm trying now to check, to see whether you changed your mind over night because you said he had. That's what is contained in your statement and that's what you confirmed yesterday, but I can see now that you managed to memorize the fact that he had not, so I just wanted to do a quick spot-check here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We have again this story about the party membership where I yesterday was quoting our proofing notes and where the witness has corrected this. Mr. Seselj is coming back again to this issue which has already been discussed yesterday. I just wanted to let this know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did know that. Continue, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the list of people to be expelled was given to me by Ostoja Sibincic and other members of the Serbian Radical Party, and that you know that for a fact. Now I want to know, how is it that you know that for a fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't want to object all the time, but Mr. Seselj should be correct. The witness did not -- I lost it now. The witness did not say that Ostoja Sibincic was giving the list. He said he assumes that Ostoja Sibincic contacted Mr. Seselj and gave him a list. It was not that clear like Mr. Seselj did this in his last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, the witness did not say that Mr. Sibincic had given you a list. He said that he believed that. It's an assumption, he is not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not correct. I jotted down here that the witness said he knew that for a fact, that the list had been provided to me by Ostoja Sibincic and other members. That's what the witness said here. Not that he thinks. He said he knew that for fact. Please refer to the transcript. He said that before he stated that he did not see me take a list from the pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let's shed some light on this immediately. Witness, did you think so, were you sure, did you see him give something? Tell us exactly what you said earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I think that the leaders, headed by Ostoja Sibincic, had provided a list of people who were to move out of Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Just to assist all of us, I think I found the quote from the transcript of yesterday. The Presiding Judge was -- and it's on page 10623, line 1. Presiding Judge is asking: "So you are telling the truth. This mean that before delivering his speech, Mr. Seselj spoke with the leaders and the leaders gave him the list." Then there is additional text here but I think is, at the moment, not important but the witness's direct answer to this is: "I'd like to say something to you. Ostoja Sibincic was Seselj's right-hand man. Most probably he contacted him every day, that is, in terms of what the situation in the village was like." So the witness made it very clear. He said "most probably," that means he did not know for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer had to read the parts that he claims are irrelevant because this is where we can see the first answer of the witness to your question, Mr. President, and the rest follows after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, what was not essential for you, I don't have the transcript here, but I trust you, tell me what is after?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I cannot summarize it because I now see it for the first time, I was using the word search or the WordWheel search. I read the sentence where you finished: "... and leaders gave him the list." Now I can read the following text: "Then he, who knows absolutely no one from this village, this is the first time that he set foot in this village just out of -- from memory. He was able to give five or ten -- between five or ten names which means that he learned five or ten names by" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I apologise. "By," and here is written "rote," so that he could actually speak them out in his speech, because in the speech that I have, he mentioned a great number of people, but people who had nothing to do with the village. For example, he mentioned members of the Communist League, Vuk Draskovic, Milan Komenic, Dragoljub Misiljevic [phoen], Zoran Djindjic, Kosta Cavoski, Nikola Milosevic. So he mentioned a great number of names, so he is very good at quoting names of people that he knows for political reasons, of course, but he didn't know the names of the villagers in the first place. That means that if you are telling the truth, he learned by rote five to ten names and then delivered them in a speech. Is this what happened?" This was the question of the Presiding Judge and the answer of the witness I already read. If you want to, I can repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... repeat it, thank you. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fair enough. So how do you know that Ostoja Sibincic was my right-hand man, and that he was in daily contact with me?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ostoja Sibincic acted in such a manner in the village. He acted like he was the boss. He was giving out the addresses of people who should --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you. I'm asking you how do you know that he was my right-hand man, and that he was in daily contact with me? That's what I'm interested in. I don't want to know what he was doing.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the assumption. That's an assumption that one makes about a man of this kind. Nobody would be surprised to hear anything about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Zvonko Paulic is?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So who is?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is my nephew.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He works in the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia in Zagreb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where does he work then?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He works in Koncar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But did he work in the Ministry of the Interior at one point?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No. He completed the high school of the interior affairs in Kamenica and then he went to Croatia and worked in the Croatian MUP.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not work there. He found a job in the Koncar factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So he never worked in MUP?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Are you sure?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, ha, ha, fine. You said that when you came to Jaksic that that is where you got this house that you swapped?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that this house had been torched, the house that you received in the swap, is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house was torched and so was the barn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How was it torched, this house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A part of the roof was burned down on the house, from the front, and there were no windows on the front because a Sagger missile had impacted there and the roof on the barn was also burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the house was not burned down, it was just damaged?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the house was inhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The house was inhabitable because Serbs were living there and they were exposed to constant abuse and were forced to move to Serbia; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who forced them to move out, but what I do know is what the house was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you will find out who made them leave soon enough. That was the house that belonged to Desanka Milosavljevic, is that right, and her husband Stjepanovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her husband Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Her husband Branko Stjepanovic and Desanka Milosavljevic. They were married but they had different surnames; is that right? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko Milosavljevic, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And since they were Serbs -- was there any fighting ever in Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since I arrived there or before my time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, before your time, from 1990 onwards, was there any fighting there, any combat activities?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that, but what I do know is that a couple of shells landed since I came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the shells or bombs landed in Serb yards and Serb houses to make them move out as soon as possible. Do you know that 28 Serb villages around Slavonska Pozega were forcibly evicted by the Croatian military?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that people moved out and I do know that my house, the house that I received in the swap was uninhabitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, your house was habitable, and as soon as you did the swap, the Croatian authorities fixed the house free of charge.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that they gave me a small loan. I had to provide two guarantors to put the roof on the house. You can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the methodology was as follows: Since nobody harassed you in Hrtkovci, you had your friends in Slavonska Pozega, you went there, and there was this large scale campaign of harassment against Serbs there, you picked a house that you liked and then an action was launched against this house. And as Desanka Milosavljevic stated to my associates, I think that her husband died in the meantime, she says that their house was targeted seven or eight times, that the barn was set on fire. They set a fire in several places and then one is supposed to put the fire out and the phone lines were cut off. This was an organised campaign to force the Serbs to move out as soon as possible. And after that happened, two or three days later, you came to their house, and you spoke to them about the swap. Desanka Milosavljevic asked you, Well, why are you leaving Hrtkovci, and you said that you were being harassed over the phone; is that right? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I could fancy a house that was burned down and to get that kind of house in exchange for two houses, one a new house and the other one slightly older. What kind of a person would I have to be if I were to accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Seselj made an investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: -- note we could not finish the interpretation because of overlapping speakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... say that you came see them. This is important, are they lying or are you lying? This is an essential element. If they are saying that you came and if you say, I never came, it means that either they are lying or you are lying. One has to be lying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday that Mr. Spasojevic came to see me and that he picked a house for Branko. And then two days later, Branko's daughter came into my house in a Lada car. She brought her son with her. There were Banja Luka plates on the Lada car and two armed civilians accompanying her. I was then given an address and I went to Pozega. And when I saw that, I realised that I had to take what was an offer because if I refused to take it, I would be destitute. I would have nothing. And that's when I signed this contract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you recognise that did you go there, you saw and you had to take up the offer because that was all that was on offer for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] She came to see me first. She moved into my house first, so I didn't have a house here and I didn't have a house there. If I refused to take the house there, then I would have nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You fabricated all this. The Stjepanovic-Milosavljevic family did not see the house in Hrtkovci when they signed the contract in Slavonska Pozega. They didn't know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know who Ilija Sutalo is?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ilija Sutalo was the key person behind the campaign to persecute Serbs in Pozega; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't know that. Well, Mrs. Desanka Milosavljevic does know that. She knows that Ilija Sutalo, as a member of Paraga's formation, the Croatian armed forces of the Croatian party of rights, would that be Paraga's formations?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I was not into politics there; I'm not into politics here either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And at the head of Paraga's formations, Ilija Sutalo organised the tax on Serb houses in order to force the Serbs to leave Slavonska Pozega and the villages around it; is that right? That's what Desanka Milosavljevic says; is that true? You don't know.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when you came to Jaksic, and after you got three times as much property as you left in Hrtkovci --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We couldn't hear the rest of the answer -- the rest of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Speak slowly, please, because the interpreters are having a difficult time. Please proceed, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I came to Pozega, I found a job in the mill, in the silo as a seasonal worker from the time when the wheat came in, the wheat harvest, to the time when the corn harvest ended. And when my contract expired, I was jobless. Ilija Sutalo had a small factory producing coils for immersion heaters and that's where I found a job. I worked there every day, eight hours a day. That was the morning shift, and that's the sum total of what I know about Ilija. He is my best man. He stood by me in church when I got married, and I'm really thankful to him for that because he made it possible for my children to receive the sacraments in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. So now you have provided me with important information, Mr. Baricevic. You got married in church quite late in life and that's where you had your children baptized; is that so? Well, relatively late in life.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had my children baptized in their proper time, that was done with the help of my wife's parents. And I told you yesterday that I had to be a member of the League of Communists in order to keep my job and those who went to church couldn't get a job, couldn't keep a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you there. But you said that in 1980, when Tito died, you returned your membership card and it took you 20 years to get married in church once you stopped being a member of the League of Communists, well, you could go to church as much as you like.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why isn't it the way it is?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because it was the same system still and people would get fired for minor transgressions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: First of all, nobody was fired because they went to church, and it was particularly impossible after Tito's death. There was not a single case in Serbia that somebody was fired, especially in the local commune, because they went to church.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were cases like that. There sure were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You invented all of that. And when you got there, and when you married your wife in church, then you said that, earlier on, you did not have the possibility of getting married because you had been prohibited from doing that; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what I said just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It took you 12 years. I'm trying to say that up until 1990, you were a member of the League of Communists and an informant of the state security service, and as such, you didn't want to go to church because you were a man of the regime in your village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I ask for relevance. What has that to do with the expulsion of Croats from Hrtkovci with the witness personal things like marriage and baptism of his children?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a small detail. You were a Catholic. From what I understand, under the communist regime, Catholics ran up against difficulties because they didn't have a job but this prevailed after Tito's death, which was a real problem. This is what I understood. Did you hear what I said? Sir, what do you have to say this, which would explain why you got married a few years later.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said clearly that I was a member of the League of Communists only for the sake of work because it was hard to get a job. I did baptise my children 150 kilometres away so the people wouldn't know about it, and I didn't dare marry in church because of my work. When I left the village, I got married. Is it a shameful thing to be a Catholic today?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not a shameful thing to be a Catholic in the times of communism either, and nobody was persecuted for their religious beliefs. But nobody could be a member of the League of Communists if they professed a religion, and also, they could not go to top leadership positions.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, in order to have someone work as a plumber or as a member of the council of the local commune, one did not really have to be a member of the League of Communists; isn't that right, Mr. Baricevic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's not what I think, I know, I experienced that. I was persecuted under that regime, but I do not allow you to present this regime a lot worse than it actually was, as if they ate little children alive. That is what you are trying to say. Now, there was a total number of 2 million members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia at the time. Do you remember that, Mr. Baricevic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Around 2 million. And the population of Yugoslavia was 21 million; right? So, 10 percent in relation to the total population were members of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. If one-third were roughly minors, then out of 14 million inhabitants of age, 2 million were members of the League of Communists. Not everybody else was unemployed and persecuted; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that's the way it was, but at any rate, in my situation I did not dare do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There is something else that makes your situation more difficult, your father's name was Ivan; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was an Ustasha during the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He was an Ustasha. I have a document of the state security service stating that he was an Ustasha. You want to see the document?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, you don't want to look at it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it wouldn't be right to bring up my dead father's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is right to mention your dead father's name if he was an Ustasha and if that charted your destiny and you had to prove yourself to be a communist that was a lot more of a communist than everybody else.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. There is not a grain of truth in what you are saying. Not a grain of truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would be grateful if Mr. Seselj could provide us with a copy of what he has there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are saying you have a document. We don't have this document. You can say anything you like. We don't have this document, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your service, if they want to, can quickly -- well, look actually, I was supposed to receive this document with an accompanying letter. This was provided to me by the state security service of Serbia through the counsel for cooperation with The Hague Tribunal at the request made by my legal advisors. However, my legal advisors provided me with a single copy. I did not prepare this as I usually do prepare everything else, because I do not have communication with my associates. However, somebody from the registry can make a copy, I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, is it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Only one speaker at a time can be interpreted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a document in B/C/S; this is a document in the Serbian language. I did not express any wish for you to read this. The Prosecutor asked for it and I am willing to make it possible to have a photocopy made. I would have prepared this on time, as I always did, if I had communication with my associates. Since I don't, I try to make do, I find this paper, that paper, but the Prosecution does have this document. It was published in that book of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj is talking about your family's past, which we know nothing about. Do you agree, do you disagree with him. If you disagree, say so, and then he will move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not agree. Absolutely not. Can I clarify something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please clarify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who were in the enemy army were in prison. My father never even saw a prison, let alone do time in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know full well that that is not true. Some of them who were captured straightaway were summarily executed, some were tried before a court and others were amnestied, pardoned, because there were several cases of pardon. Probably no one carried out an investigation or the investigation did not come to the conclusion that your father had personally committed crimes. He was not tried, but he had been a member of the Ustasha formations and this was a nightmare for you and that made you be much more of a communist than people usually were. You wanted to prove that you were a greater Catholic than the pope as it were. That is the core of the matter. That is why I believe that you were so firm in your communist beliefs and why you were an informant of the state security service.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, there is not a grain of truth in any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right, then. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of this is a pure fabrication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps the state security service is fabricating things. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, let us deal with the agreement on the exchange of moveable and immovable property. You concluded this contract with Ranko Milosavljevic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Branko Milosavljevic and Stanka Stjepanovic; right? On the one hand is Branko Milosavljevic, Stanka Stjepanovic and their daughter Branka; right? And the other side is you and your wife, Elizabeta Baricevic. Your signature is on the contract; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is the case?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one side it is me and my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. Elizabeta is your mother; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, this is the property that you are exchanging or swapping from Branko Milosavljevic and his family you are receiving land, 1 hectare, 38 acres, and 89 square metres of land. Please follow me carefully and correct me if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution has this contract. They could have presented it to you here, Judges. Why they didn't, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then also 22 acres and 98 square metres of arable lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We don't have the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: -- just for the information of everybody here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't have the document, very well. Please proceed. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see Mr. President, this lack of seriousness. They proof a witness, they prepare him for six years to testify in my trial, to accuse me of persecuting Croats in Hrtkovci. This is a witness who exchanged his property and went to Slavonska Pozega, and it didn't cross their mind to get the contract on the exchange of property and immovable property which would be the key evidence here. Should I continue with this? Should I just provide this information, what it was that they provided, that is to say, this family of Branko Milosavljevic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm sorry, but I was still listening to the translation. I believe you are the person who needs this for your cross-examination. You have conducted an in-depth investigation as regards this witness. Maybe you could have -- have this document admitted. I would have been quite happy with that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Judge, the contract was published in that book of mine. Since my communication with my legal associates has been severed, I don't have the original of the contract. They have it, though. And I am now using the contract that was published in the book. I have it here. I have a copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not abridged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... an interpretation of your last words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Only one speaker can be interpreted at a time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My fellow Judge said that the communications were not cut, but that you were the person that interrupted all form of communication. In any case, there is a pending motion regarding this particular issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thirdly, [B/C/S spoken] arable land, 1 hectare and 10 square metres. Follow me carefully. [B/C/S spoken] meadow, 28 acres. [B/C/S spoken] meadow, 28 acres, 31 square metres. [B/C/S spoken] meadow, 9 square metres and 2 hectares, a house and the land surrounding it, 23 acres and 98 square metres. Then [B/C/S spoken] land of 59 acres and 34 square metres. Is that the property that was given to you by Branko Milosavljevic's family in exchange for your property? Did I read it out right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There are things missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is missing?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gromulja.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Gromulja is missing?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where is this Gromulja?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That was not in your contract, you managed to extort that with the assistance of the Croatian authorities after you moved there. I have that judgement here as well because you claimed, or, rather, when they were no longer in Croatia, when they were not even informed of the fact that these proceedings were ongoing, you said that you were not given this land of Gromulja, and then the court granted it to you with the explanation that this was omitted from the contract by mistake. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that Stanka came to my house. She was the daughter of Branko and Desanka. I went to Pozega to see what was there and what did I see. We went to see the lawyer Primorac, and she drew up a contract. Mistakenly she omitted -- well, was it intentional or not, I don't know, but she was Stanka's friend. Let me tell you that Stanka was a judge in Pozega, and this woman was a lawyer. Now, I don't want to make any assertions as to whether this was done intentionally or unwittingly, but there is one thing that is important and that is that Desanka, Stanka's mother, made me the owner of every one of the fields there. I did not even see that this little part was missing. Only a month later, she sent me new contract from Pozega. She gave it to Cacic, and this had to do with this small field, and he asked for 5.000 Deutschemark, and they took me to court. I objected to the court and I brought in witnesses who went along with me when the woman was making me the owner of all of this. So that is the whole story.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, we have heard the witness at great lengths. Contrary to what you are saying, he is not the person who instituted the legal proceedings but the other party, this is what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what he said, Mr. President. I don't know what kind of interpretation you are receiving. Listen, a contract was concluded here. It's a very specific one and it gives the exact numbers of the land that is being exchanged. What one party is providing, what the other party is providing. When all of that was completed, when this Serb family left Slavonska Pozega and went to Hrtkovci, when Mr. Baricevic became the owner of this property, then he appeared as a plaintiff before the Croatian court, and he asked for yet another field of 1 hectare and 70 acres. It was owned by Stanka Milosavljevic-Stjepanovic. That field had not been the object of this exchange. Stanka had not been informed at all of these court proceedings. It was only 12 years later that she found out that that had happened and she asked for a retrial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Mr. Seselj is saying that you are the person who instituted these legal proceedings before the Croatian court. Was it you or was it the other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I gave you my answer. Mr. Cacic from Pozega came to see me, he had a contract and he asked me to give him 5.000 Deutschemarks, and he filed a legal suit against me in court for compensation of damage. And because I had witnesses for the handover of the property, I brought those witnesses, I called those witnesses to indicate that that is what she did and that's what she originally wanted to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who were those witnesses, Mr. Baricevic? Were they Nikola Lulic, Ante Grizelj and Marko Kalic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Grizelj. Ante Stipic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And who else?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it seems to me that it was also Ilija Sutalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ilija Sutalo, Ante Grizelj, Nikola Lulic, and Marko Kalic. Marko Kalic came from Hrtkovci together with you. And you, together with them, joined this Paraga's party formation that continued to persecute Serbs in Pozega; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes it is. Yes it is. Now let us see, what is it that you gave in return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, witness. Mr. Seselj is stating something which can be important. He is saying that you joined the Paraga formations. Is this true, not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not true. I was not in any kind of army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't say that you were in an army. You took part in the activities of this terrorist group that continued to torture the properties, to fire shots at their house, to harass Serbs, and to speed up their departure from Pozega.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you are stating this. Do you have any evidence, any proof, any documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... from the state security service, where it says that Zvonko Paulic also took part in that. He is the son of this witness's sister. He was a member of the Croatian MUP and that he went as far as to bring some Serbs to the new house of this witness and they were mistreated and harassed there in order to be forced to flee Slavonska Pozega. This is what is it says in a document from the state security service, and the Prosecutor can check over the phone in Belgrade whether this is an original document that I have in my hand. He can call the counsel for cooperation with the Tribunal to check whether I did receive a document from the state security service about Franja Baricevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have two issues, the accused is alleging that the witness has allegedly committed crimes. He should, in my system at least, he should be cautioned that he is not obliged to answer these things. And another thing, a little observation, I've been here in court several times, I have only one time got from Mr. Seselj in advance documents he was using in cross-examination and that was at the end of the examination-in-chief, and I got it in B/C/S. I think this approach is completely unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, normally speaking, since you do not ask any of your documents to be admitted, normally speaking, the Prosecution should have a copy of all the documents you are going to be using during your cross-examination beforehand. But since you did not ask these documents to be admitted, we face a void. Please proceed. You have five minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me remind you, Mr. President, that I have always provided the documents in advance, both to the Prosecution and to the Trial Chamber, while I was able to cooperate with my legal advisors. Once a stop was put to that, I have been unable to continue doing so. But 15 to 20 days ago, I handed this book to the Prosecution, this whole book, and then the Prosecution informed me that they are already working on this book and that they intend to charge me with contempt of court because of this book. And after I could no longer cooperate with my legal advisors, I have been unable to provide documents in advance, but that's not my fault. I used to do that always. But as far as translation is concerned, that's not my concern. Translating documents into English and French. That's really not my concern. I don't want to concern myself about it. I am guaranteed right to use my own mother tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Another little observation. In my system, it's completely unlawful to publish statements given to the Prosecution and which I expected to be used in court. It is the reason for these regulations, and I know that it is in several European countries the same, is not to influence the witness. My assumption that Mr. Seselj is publishing these statements already much in advance and slamming the witnesses who are coming here in court. He has a specific reason to do this and as I don't want to speculate. Everybody should conclude what the reason might be for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not difficult for you to check. You can check in the Croatian MUP whether there is a single note about me there in their files. What Seselj is saying about me, this is just lies, pure and simple. I state this here with full responsibility, here as I sit before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj. It's been recorded on the transcript. Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Baricevic, please follow closely. I will now list the property that you gave in exchange. The property that you had in Hrtkovci. It's a house, an arable land and yard, the size is 6 acres, 42 square metres. Then another stretch of arable land, 17 acres and 90 square metres. Then [B/C/S spoken] arable land, 68 acres, 31 square metres. [B/C/S spoken] arable land, 1 hectare, 13 acres, 9 square metres. And your mother gave arable land in Sicara [phoen], the size was 75 acres, 66 square metres. And you together, you and your mother gave an orchard; the size is 14 acres, 52 square metres; orchard 7 acres, 37 square metres; and orchard, 8 acres, 92 square metres. Is that right? Did I read everything?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not so. What is missing here, it says only one house whereas -- well, what does it mean if you give an orchard in exchange for meadow? If you are smart, you can figure this out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But the question is what state this orchard was in; is that not so, Mr. Baricevic?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The orchard was in good state while it was in good hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was a very bad state, Mr. Baricevic. Now, as you concluded this contract, you determined that the value of both properties was 800.000 Croatian dinars; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And there is a provision in that contract that this exchange is entered into voluntarily and there shall be no further payments made by any parties, is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what it says in the contract, then that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And this is a contract that was entered into before the Croatian authorities, it is registered before a Croatian court?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just say that only one house is listed here. Where is the other house?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the other house was torn down as soon as the Milosavljevic Stjepanovic family came to Hrtkovci because it was completely unusable. It was an old adobe house, nobody could live there.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this house stands there today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That house is unusable.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stanka's mother lives in that house and Stanka lives in the new house that I built, the one with the attic. I know that very well. Nobody can tell me anything about that. I'm sure about what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, let's see what Stanka has to say about that. She says that they gave you a house in Slavonska Pozega which was a surface of 110 square metres; is that right? Does it have 110 square metres?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How much -- what is the surface then?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The surface is 95 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Stanka Stjepanovic, in her statement, says 110 square metres, fully completed and furnished with parquet floors and tiles and furniture. Did you find any furniture in that house?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'll go straight to the point. You have a contract, a contract has been described at length, so now the other part of the contract is talked about. Were you victimized in this exchange or were you the beneficiary? This is a question I put to you. From what I understood, the Defence is saying that you were the beneficiary and not the other people. What do you have to say to that? Were you victimized or were you the beneficiary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me say this once again, that I left behind a house and Stjepanovic was already in that house. I came to the house where Desanka and her husband were. That house had been torched. I left two houses. One was a new house built in 1983, the other one was built in 1953. I signed the contract because I didn't want to lose everything. I didn't want to be left out in the street. And now it is up to you to judge who is losing here, who is the war profiteer here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whatever the case may be, it is difficult to establish who the winner and the loser is. For this to happen, the two properties would have had to be assessed. We don't have the contract because the Prosecution in its -- in the presentation of its case did not show us the contract, and Mr. Seselj is not going to admit the document. We are going to have a break and resume in 20 minutes time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Please replace not abridged by not interrupted

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. And I take this opportunity to welcome the new arrivals in the OTP. Mrs. Biersay, for example, very happy to see you. Mr. Seselj, you have 50 minutes left and you have the floor. 50 not 15. 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that I won't talk all of those 50 minutes that I have to complete my cross-examination. Mr. Baricevic, you see there is an interesting sentence in the statement that Desanka Milosavljevic made. She says that all the rich Croats remained in Hrtkovci, those who owned a lot of land, whereas those Croats who were poorer, less well off, and who had this opportunity to pick and choose much better things than they left behind in Hrtkovci. What do you think about this statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have already explained to this Chamber what I had owned and what kind of situation I encountered in Jaksic. Now, as to who remained and under what conditions and for what reasons, I would not go into that. I know that some rich people left, some rich people stayed, and all I take care of is myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And of the rich Croats from Hrtkovci, who left?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there are those but you don't know their names?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Tell me this, if we bear in mind that until mid-1992, 200.000 Serbs were expelled from Croatia, and when we take into account the 200.000 that were expelled in 1995, that is the figure of 400.000 Serbs expelled from Croatia and only a few thousand Croats left Serbia. Now, if we look at this in purely economic terms, if we set aside the horrible ways in which Serbs were persecuted in Croatia and the Tribunal in The Hague refused to prosecute those who are responsible for it, let us look at the economic aspect. We have the law of supply and demand on the market. For -- first 200.000, then 400.000 Serbs are looking for somebody to exchange their property, their shops, their small factories with; and on the other side, you have just a few thousand Croats. Who is in a better position here when it comes to this exchange, because the logic of the law of economics tells us that those who are in demand are in a better position on the market than those who offer what they have to offer in vain; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what my situation was, how I fared in this exchange. I lost a brand new house, and it takes two generations to build it. My father and myself, we worked hard for that and I lost that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you would not venture into this economic -- logic of economics, the law of supply and demand, you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let's not get into economic logic. It's true that if we have a market with 400.000 people on the supply side on the one hand, and a few thousand on the other side, on the demand side, then that could be a bit strange. But what I'm interested in your answer is the following: I think I understand now that all Croats from Hrtkovci didn't leave. Some of them stayed in Hrtkovci, which is important. But what I'm interested in is the following: Among the Croats who left, it seems that there were some rich Croats who actually stayed and the lesser well off seemed to have left. But as far as you remember, could you tell us how many Croats stayed in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said yesterday that 460 families moved out from Hrtkovci, and 300 families within a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many stayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, roughly speaking, maybe 6 or 7 per cent remained.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, we will have a demographer here and we can discuss it with her, because this witness is not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Baricevic, after you left for Jaksic, you went back to Hrtkovci how many times did you go back to Hrtkovci after your departure?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how many times did Desanka Milosavljevic and her daughter, Stanka Stjepanovic, go to Jaksic, to Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I did not get into touch with them, they didn't get in touch with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And is it the usual situation for Croats who lived in Serbia to be able to go back to Serbia much more often and it is much easier for them as opposed to the Serbs who were expelled who don't dare go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that, but I really was quite apprehensive about going to visit my father's grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
