utterances.text: But in the end you did there and you didn't have any problems?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fair enough. That's very important. Do you know how many thousands of Serb houses were destroyed throughout Croatia, not in combat zones, outside of the combat zones, in Split, in Sibenik, in Zadar, in mainland Croatia. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to see in Pozega and around it, the houses were destroyed, but now they have been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many empty Serb houses still remain throughout Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you know about any Croat houses in Serbia that were torn down, about an instance when somebody came and destroyed somebody's house because that somebody was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know if any Croats were deported from Serbia? Do you know what it means to deport somebody? The authorities or some other armed group captures you and forces you to leave, and you have to leave all your property behind. Was any Croat expelled from Serbia and were forced to leave their property behind?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were some cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For instance, Jurcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where was he expelled from?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who expelled him?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who expelled him, but he left after I did and he came without anything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are kindly asked to make pauses between questions and answers. A few questions and answers are missing, note the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How can you say that he was expelled? How can you say that he was expelled and you don't know who expelled him and how?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he entered an apartment and he is building himself a house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wait a moment. That is not proof of him being evicted from somewhere. Did he have a house in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What happened to that house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean left it, did he sell the house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He just left the house and the house just stayed on?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess somebody moved in. I'm saying that this happened after I had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, I guess. Never mind, I don't want you to say things like "I guess." Is it correct that in addition to this house in Jaksic of 110 square metres, did you get a shed that is between 60 and 70 square metres?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shed was on four pillars. There wasn't even any concrete there, just four pillars, and there wasn't a proper roof either, that's the exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Perhaps. You also got a big building in the yard with ainfort, and Stanka told me that this is a big door through which one enters the economic part of the yard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a classical passageway in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on. Also that you found their sheds, pigsties, chicken coops, smoking huts, and buildings for cattle fodder, and things like that; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every farmhouse is supposed to have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: This is not every farmhouse. This was the house that belonged to this very prominent farmer, and everything was at the highest technological level, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I would not go into all of that without checking properly what the state of the house was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Speakers are overlapping again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the situation in Hrtkovci, you just --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's wait for us to get to Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj and Mr. Witness do not overlap because it is impossible for the interpreters to catch, and then we don't understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of these fields was right by the asphalt road, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is tilling land.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And it is very convenient for breaking it up into smaller plots for building houses?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is arable land.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But Stanka Stjepanovic says that it is 100.000 Euro worth.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when all the public utilities get there, but that will be in about ten years or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But it is very valuable and you cannot consider it be -- well, even to this day, you wouldn't just sell it as arable land.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is being sold as arable land.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Nobody is trying to sell it now. Everybody is waiting to sell it for big money. Also you got a tractor that was bought just before the war broke out with all the necessary machinery and accessories; am I right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you are not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They left you all the furniture and everything they had in the house; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And from -- and you took everything from Hrtkovci from your house and you left an empty house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what is true then, they took everything and you left everything behind?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again, I would like to repeat this. This departure of ours -- I mean, this going back from Jaksic to Hrtkovci, when I signed this contract with Mira Primorac, I had to go back in order to give Stanka the contract to have it confirmed in Ruma. And then, yet again, I went back, or rather, in Jaksic, Branko and Desanka were still there, and I went back and my daughter -- or, rather, their daughter was in the house as I was going between the two houses. And Ante Grizelj and I, on one occasion, took this little truck and we divided this up in half, this is one half, this is the other half, are you going to load it or will I, and then we loaded on to this little truck the most basic clothing and two couches. The house was full, or, rather, both houses were full, the refrigerators were there, everything else. When I returned to Jaksic through Hungary, then I unloaded these bits and pieces that I brought in. Desanka loaded a full truck, that full truck, and went to Hrtkovci. Now that is the whole truth. That can be confirmed not only by one person, but by 20 persons who know about this. They know that I had no bed to lie in until I brought in my things because they had taken everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is it true that you did not leave a single agricultural machine in Hrtkovci that was in operational order?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you found in Jaksic all the agricultural machinery you needed that was in proper working order? You left an old tractor and you found a perfectly new one?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm checking. All right. I have Mrs. Stanka Stjepanovic's statement, and now I'm checking with you what is true and what is not true. Well, the very fact that not at any point in time did you look me in the eye is telling enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This tractor, when you arrived, was there a tractor? Yes or no? Had they left a tractor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a tractor there, but then I had left my tractor behind too. So one tractor for another tractor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us the make of this tractor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] IMT. A small one, 35 horsepower. And it was manufactured in 1969.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did it work? Did it operate properly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It worked properly, normally. If you maintain it properly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can imagine, Mr. President, how well a tractor that is 23 years old works.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one I talked about now is the one that I found in Jaksic, what I talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. This is what Mrs. Stanka Stjepanovic says, that in Hrtkovci they found an old, dilapidated house of 60 square metres. So you got a house of 110 square metres and you gave a house of 60 square metres; right? How big was your house in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, I said yesterday that my new house, with an attic at that, was of the following dimensions: 11 by 12. Whereas the old house -- just a moment, please. It was 8 by 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Wow, a palace, sir. A palace. 8 by 15.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: 120 square metres, the foundation?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And out buildings too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The house that you called your new house, does yours have a parquet floor at all?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but floor heating.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was no floor heating. There was concrete there, and then you plastered some kind of wall-to-wall carpeting on the concrete. Is that what you call parquet flooring?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying it's not parquet flooring but it was heated floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean heated floors?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Using electricity?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Using water.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What do you mean water?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, maybe you might move on to something else. You should move on to something else. We'll never know unless the Trial Chamber goes on site to check out your old house and the house you obtained through swapping. I don't have any time for this. I'm sitting on two trials every day, I don't have any time to go on site. But if I had had time, I would have invited my fellow Judges to go and check things on site. Maybe the Prosecutor, during the investigation, could also have taken pictures of your old house and the new one, could have been done. If we had had pictures, you know, we could have compared. But we have nothing, so I don't think that we can draw any final conclusion out of all this. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This old house, as you've been calling it, according to Stanka Stjepanovic's testimony, was torn down as soon as they arrived because it could not be used. And also they had to adapt the house that you call the new one to make it liveable.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a pure lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Fine, fine. It's obvious here who is lying and who is not lying. It's very obvious here. The very fact that you are not able to look me in the eye when answering my questions is very telling, as far as I'm concerned, and I'm a great psychologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't intimidate the witness. You have your own version, he's got his own. The Judges will decide.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, all right. If you consider this to be intimidation, then I'm not going to say that to him again. But it's all right if he says lie, whereas I'm not allowed to say lie even when something is the most blatant possible lie. But anyway, who do I have to blame.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know who Marko Kalic is?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He arrived in Jaksic too; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He also swapped houses with Jovo Njemcevic; right? Do you know that he swapped houses with him?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that he swapped houses, but I don't know the name of the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, his name is Jovo Njemcevic and he gave a statement to me about his own fate. He was also subjected to attacks there. Ilija Sutalo led this group of Croats, he says that too. They were torching and blowing up Serb houses, harassing people and causing a great deal of unrest, and then Marko Kalic came to him after having gone through all this harassment, and then he made this offer to swap houses. Since Jovo Njemcevic had lived there on his own, his daughter and son-in-law lived in Belgrade, they were concerned about him and they decided to swap houses, or, rather, property with Kalic. Jovo Njemcevic says that he went to the Pozega SUP with Kalic and that that's where he got a proper emigration document allowing him to leave Croatia, but he could no longer go back to Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you enter Croatia without a certificate from the local parish priest that you had been baptized in the local church?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could enter, but I could not exercise my rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What rights?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, say, get married, then, well, to have my children receive the holy communion and the sacrament.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Before leaving Hrtkovci, you obtained a certificate from the local parish priest, Niko Kraljevic, that you had been baptized a Roman Catholic at the church there; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When later?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, later. Later. A man brought this to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What was this man who brought this to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I have to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You do have to say.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stipo Roland.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where did he bring that from, Hrtkovci to Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What passport did you use for entering Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the Yugoslav passport.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The passport of the SFRY, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It hadn't been changed in Serbia yet, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the Croatian authorities no longer recognised that passport. With that passport one could leave Croatia but one could not enter Croatia with that passport?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. The passport was valid and one could travel with it for as long as it was valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution showed us proof here that one could not enter Croatia without a certificate issued by local parish priests to the effect that a person belonged to the Roman Catholic church?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did enter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, you entered. All right. And he complains that in Jaksic he had a big proper house, property, valuable machinery and that in Hrtkovci he found a dilapidated house of 60 square metres. Do you know what kind of a house Marko Kalic had in Hrtkovci? He is your neighbour, you'd have to know.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the best answer would be for you to ask Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would I ask him, I'm asking you. You know. You know where Marko lived.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the house but I never entered the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You saw this house in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of a house was it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a house is a house. It has a gate, it has a door, it is painted, it has a roof and what kind of material it was made of, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Oh, you don't know. Well, then, fine, let me believe you on that. Katica Paulic is your sister, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your very own sister?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: She moved to Zagreb, right, from Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know when she moved, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that she moved after I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I moved in May, and then she perhaps moved out in late May, early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of a house did she have in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had a house, I know that very well, because my father and I helped her build the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of a house was it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had an attic. It had a cellar. The dimensions were 10 by -- I don't know, 9 by -- 9 or 10, never mind. And in front there was a shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of a house did she get in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zagreb, she got a house at Zitnjak. In Ivanja [phoen] -- no, no, not Ivanja. She got this tiny little house. This year, she had to build a new roof because the old roof almost fell on her head. It was so rotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How could that be?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Dragutin Spiric, a Serb from Zagreb, is who swapped houses with her.

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: His house is 4 kilometres away from Zagreb, Zitnjak, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: That's what Dragutin Spiric says. I don't know. I don't know. I visited Zagreb several times but I don't know it very well, perhaps you know it better; is that true?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Zagreb, yes, but not 4 kilometres away from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: He says it's 4 kilometres away from the centre. Is it closer to the centre?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is further away from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Further on he says that this was a big, well-appointed house and that in the house in Hrtkovci he found only concrete and that his wife was in tears when she realized what she had come to. And then soon after that, he died. He had an apoplexy. All of this was very difficult for him. So, feeling so sad and desperate, he died. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he died, but I knew that the house was well appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You knew that it was well appointed. Was Katica Paulic expelled from Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think she was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You think. But do you consider yourself to be a thinker of some sort? And Katica left for Zagreb on her own, she swapped her house, and her husband and her son remained living in Serbia for a time; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How is it not so when her son went to the high school of the interior affairs in Sremska Kamenica and her husband stayed with him there until he could complete his secondary education and then get a job Croatian MUP?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they moved later, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: No, no. They waited for the son to complete his training, so Katica went first and then her son and her husband joined her; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, if you say that it isn't, I think it would be pointless for me to continue asking you question this is this vein because I'm sure that everything is quite clear on the basis of your answer so far. I have completed my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Is there any redirect the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have only one short question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, yesterday you were asked by Mr. Seselj, you were asked by Mr. Seselj about Chetniks. He said, well, and it is on page 10666, line 11, and the wording is: "Well, they wore Chetniks caps and they shouted, 'This is Serbia, this is Serbia.'" This is was your answer. Mr. Seselj says: "Why do you bother about Chetnik caps? These are traditional Serbian insignias." And he was also referring to songs which these Chetniks sang. Can you explain us what Chetnik for you meant at that time? Were you informed about history, about the reputation of Chetniks? Can you explain this please, to us?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, when I was in elementary school, we were taught history, and the way we were taught history, Chetniks and Ustashas were the enemies of the Yugoslav people. That's the way I was brought up. And when I saw that, I found it quite horrifying, and I forgot to mention yesterday one thing. When I saw on Franjo Magoc's wall, a song, some lines from a song, well, Croats, there is a deep hole waiting at the end of the line for you. For a peaceful village, this was really a big deal and on the Catholic church, you could see the four C -- four S signs and you could see the letter U painted on the walls of the houses. It was a great shock. Not only for me but for the people as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you and the other inhabitants of Hrtkovci been scared about all this, what happened?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, they were scared. You go to bed in fear. You don't know who is going to live to see the morning. While my children were at home, I didn't sleep downstairs. I went to sleep up in the attic to guard my children while they were at home, and that's what forced me to take my kids out of the school before the end of the school year and to move them, to take them to my wife's parents to a safe place. I didn't do that on a whim. I did it because I was afraid. I was concerned for their lives, the life of my wife and, in the final analysis, my own life.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection, Judges. I didn't want to object before the witness replied, but this is a general objection. I would like to tell you that the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia rehabilitated Chetniks led by General Drazen Mihajlovic, as an anti-fascist formation from the Second World War. So you have the subjective picture of the Chetniks and the picture that was painted of Chetniks by the communists, and there is the whole other thing which is the objective truth, historical truth about Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This is no answer for the reasons the inhabitants had to be scared [sic]. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. Baricevic. And, Your Honours, I have no further questions. I have finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have one small question. I was very interested by your answer. You said that you were in grade school and that you were taught that the enemies of the Yugoslav people were the Chetniks and the Ustashi. This is what you were taught in school, you were told that the enemies of the Yugoslav people were the Chetniks and the Ustasha?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you were raised in that belief then, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While Tito was alive, there were no Chetniks, there were no Ustashas. It was prohibited to sing the songs of either side, and that's the way I was taught and that's the way I lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you sing, yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were songs that were not nationalist songs that you could sing, but nationalist songs could not be sung.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Witness. I have two small questions for you and I realise that you may already have answered them, and in that case, I just ask for your indulgence. But the first question I had was regarding the bus full of black-uniformed men who came just before Mr. Seselj was about to give his speech on the 6th of May, 1992, in Hrtkovci. We have spoken at length about who these soldiers were, and you told us that you were told by others that they were White Eagles. And so this remains still an open question because we have no further proof of whether or not they were actually members of the White Eagles. This is why I want to ask you if you noticed any insignia on the uniforms or any caps that they were wearing, or any other visible traces that could support your opinion that they were members of the White Eagles. Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The caps, well, those people did not wear the kind of caps that were worn by the army as it was at the time. They wore caps with the cockades, whereas the army and the police, at that time, bore a five-point stars as their insignia, and they had the cockades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, if I understand you correctly, the soldiers who came to Hrtkovci on the 6th of May, they were having cockades shown in their hats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What sort of hats or caps were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a military style cap. It was black, but instead of the five pointed star, there was the cockade that was stuck on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I see. So it was not fur -- fur hats. It was a military --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, it was not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And did they have any -- did you notice if they had any insignia on their uniforms, other than what they had on their hat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The other question I have for you, and again I apologise if you have already told us so but it may have simply slipped my mind, is whether you had a chance to see the house in Jaksic before you were forced to enter into -- before you signed the contract for exchange. Did you actually have a chance to see and assess the property that you were exchanging for your own two houses in Hrtkovci, or did you do that without having seen the new property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said at one point that when Stanka Stjepanovic came into my house, I went to Croatia and I found her parents in that house. The windows were boarded up. There were no -- there was no window panes. The barn was burned down and the roof on the house was also burnt. But I signed the contract because at the time people were already living in my house and they were living in this house here, so if I didn't sign the contract, I was -- I stood to lose everything because that was the system in Hrtkovci. If somebody got into your house, it was difficult to evict them. And that's why I agreed to the swap. I knew that I had much more, but what could I do? My children, my wife were already in Croatia. I didn't have a house at all. My children had to go to school. They had to complete that school year. I was forced to sign the contract. The villagers who came to see me told me flabbergasted, Franja, how could you do this swap, but I had to do it, that was my fate, and I fixed this house. I am still fixing it and I will bring it up to the standard that I had where -- in the house that I left, in a couple of years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was there any possibility of you, once you had moved into the new house in Croatia, to move on to another house somewhere else in Croatia? Had that been possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry, I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I am sorry. My question was, if it was possible once you had moved into the house in Jaksic in Croatia, whether you could move on from there to another house in Croatia and perhaps a better house? Was that a possibility or were you simply stuck with the house in Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What possibility? When I signed the contract for that house, and I forgot to mention that Stanka, this very same Stanka who is now living in my house, sold a house in Pozega, pocketed the money, and entered my new house and that house was not new, the one that you described as new is not new. That was an old house, built in the 1960s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, to finish.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to draw your attention to two things. The five-pointed star was removed from police uniforms in 1991. That was official. And the cockade was put on the caps with the Serbian flag, and from military uniforms the five-pointed star was removed in early 1992, as soon as General Veljko Kadijevic resigned as the Defence minister, because he had opposed this. And I would also like to note that Stanka Stjepanovic, as the witness himself admitted, was a judge in Slavonska Pozega. As a judge, she had to leave Slavonska Pozega and to flee to Serbia. I would like to draw your attention to those two important elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think the record is not correct. I was answering to Mr. Seselj at page 62, line 10, and my answer is written down there as: "This is no other reason for all inhabitants to be scared." What I think I said and I wanted to say is, this is no reason not to be scared. This should be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We'll make the correction. Thank you. Mr. -- well, witness, you have just finished your testimony. I thank you for having come to answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution, the Defence, and the Bench. I wish you a safe journey home. And I will ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall also ask the registrar to move into closed session and drop the blinds for the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we need a private session to start with.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session now, Your Honours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will start by reading the short summary of the witness evidence. The witness is a Croat who lived with his parents in the village of Hrtkovci until they were forced to leave in August 1992. The relations between different ethnic communities in Hrtkovci were harmonious, mixed marriages were perceived as normal. The problems began after 6 May 1992. The witness describes the activities of the members of the SRS before and after 6 May 1992. In particular, the involvement in expulsion of the Croats from Hrtkovci. During the autumn of 1991 and spring of 1992, a large number of Serbian refugees came to Hrtkovci. The arrival of these Serbian refugees was organised by the SRS. The local SRS must have had help from persons in higher positions in Belgrade. Ostoja Sibincic organised the so-called exchange of houses in Hrtkovci. The Serbian refugees who arrived in the village went to Sibincic to get addresses of Croat houses which they would occupy. Sibincic would provide these refugees with the necessary information to locate the house and to evict the Croatian occupants. At the beginning of 1992, the witness saw armed Chetnik groups meeting at a bar in the centre of Hrtkovci. The Chetniks carried automatic guns and knives and they wore peaked caps with Kokardas on the front. The local Croats felt intimidated by the presence of these Chetnik volunteers in their village. Seselj came to Hrtkovci on 6 May 1992. During his speech, Seselj read a list of names in public and stated that the Croats would have to leave with only plastic bags in their hands. The witness was informed by other people that Seselj read a list of names of prominent Croats who were to be expelled. Seselj also said that the children born from mixed marriages were to be killed. From 6 May 1992 onwards, the atmosphere became hostile for the Croats in Hrtkovci. There were threats that Croats would be killed if they did not leave their houses. Some Croats received telephone threats. Groups of men would go harassing the villagers in order to convince the villagers to leave and exchange their house. The witness mentioned groups of 20 Serbians who went and kicked Croats out of their houses. The police would protect the perpetrators instead of the owners of the houses. Bomb threats were also frequent. Serbian refugees would go directly to the houses where Croats lived and tell them to give up their houses. In June 1992, the witness's relative was killed. As a result of the death of his relative and the exchange of houses by his immediate neighbours, the witness decided to leave Hrtkovci. The witness and his parents packed their belongings and left for Croatia. They finally settled in Jaksic where the witness arranged the exchange of his house with a Serbian who still lives in Hrtkovci. Your Honour, that concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, now ask the traditional questions, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Before we discuss the Exhibit 65 number 5044, Mr. Witness, did you give a statement in 2002 to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Thank you. And in 2005, did you certify this statement before representatives of the registrar of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity to review your written statement in your own language?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Usher, could you please hand out the hard copy of the statement 65 ter 5044 -- questions to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at the third page with number 0465-6591, which is the first page of the English version with number -- ERN number 0189-8834. Witness, do you see your signature?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: And if you could flip through those other pages --

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Do you have your initials at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Witness, could you look at page 7, the number is 0465-6595 --

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: -- which -- page of the English version with ERN number 0189-8839. Witness do you see your signatures?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see my signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: And does that statement accurately reflect your recollection of the events described in it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Witness, if you were asked the same questions today, will you have -- will it be a reflection of your account?

utterances.speaker: FRANJA BARICEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would move for the admission under seal of this document, 65 ter number 5044.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Trial Chamber will decide after we have put a few questions to the witness. Do you have any questions to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have a few questions for you, using your statement as a basis for these questions. Regarding what happened before May 6, 1992, before Mr. Seselj's speech, could you please tell us whether in your village there were political parties that you are aware of or were you totally unaware of the political parties that existed in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said in my statement, I did not really know about this very well, but I do know that it was the SDP there that was the strongest party, that was the Social Democratic Party, then the SPO, and then this other party, just a moment, please, the Croatian party led by Bela Tonkovic and the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me discuss the Serbian Radical Party. How did you know that the Serbian Radical Party existed before May 6, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what, it's a small place. People know all these things. Sibincic was bragging and he and Aco Ejic, as far as I know, established --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... I believe that there is a problem with the microphone, witness, because it's very difficult to hear. Mrs. Biersay, is that the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's interpretation that's missing, at least for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's start over again. Regarding the Serbian Radical Party, according to you, who was member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of the SRS? There were new people there who had already exchanged houses. There was Ostoja Sibincic and this group around him. I didn't know exactly who the members were but it was his friends, people who were like minded. You never could tell because it's not that I ever saw a list so that I would know exactly who all the members of the Serb Radical Party were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know Sibincic? Did you discuss with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I never talked to him, but I knew him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You knew him but you never spoke to him. Very well. Who told you that Sibincic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party? Was it hearsay? Did you know that it was -- did somebody really tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it wasn't only a question of rumours. For example, when he spoke in taverns and public places, he showed it himself. But not directly in some contact with me. You would hear people talking about this, you'd hear him talking. You'd stand at a bit of a distance and you'd hear him talking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So that is what he said. On May 6, 1992, Mr. Seselj came to Hrtkovci to make a speech. Where were you on that day, on May 6, 1992? It seems that you did not attend the speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That day I was in the watermelon and melon fields.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Obviously you would rather be in the field with melons and watermelons than listen to Mr. Seselj. Fine. But the speech, had you heard about it beforehand or were you told about it afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about that speech later, after it was actually made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What exactly were you told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was told that the names of eminent Croats from the village were read out and it was stated that they had to move out. Also, that it was said at this gathering that mixed marriages should be divorced, that the children should be killed. It is people from mixed marriages who talked about this the most. They were the ones who complained about it the most. They were moaning about what was wrong with their children, why would they have to be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember if someone from a mixed marriage told you that? As far as you recollect, can you give us a name or not? It did happen a long time ago and I fully understand that you would not really remember who said what to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I cannot remember exactly. I cannot remember the names and I wouldn't like to mention them either. After all, these are people from mixed marriages, and from time to time, they go to Hrtkovci so I'm afraid for their safety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you did not attend the speech. And you can only tell us what people told you. Now, let's move to the core of your -- the main element of your statement, which is the house exchange. Can you tell us how it happened? To start with, can you describe your own house in Hrtkovci, how many rooms it had, what size it was? Could you describe your house to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was a house that was similar to the one that I swapped it for. It is only natural that we cannot exchange houses for an absolutely identical house. It was a house, say, with three rooms, a kitchen, a pantry, a bathroom, and then the smaller buildings outside. They are as big as they are. You cannot really have an ideal swap. I exchanged my house, tractor, all my agricultural machinery and land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a three-room house with a kitchen, bathroom, and there was some agricultural land and a tractor. Let's talk about the agricultural land. Could you tell us what was the acreage where you were planting those watermelons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I only planted watermelons and melons. All other crops were there too. It was over 7 hectares, my land was, and I got around 6 hectares.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 7 hectares. Very well, now we have a good idea of the size of this agricultural land. How was the exchange going to take place, what happened, who told you to do what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, how did this exchange take place. People kept coming to the village and offering exchanges of houses to us. They gave us addresses in Croatia and made offers to us to go there and see for ourselves, and, for example, there was even a little ad by the shop saying that there were 30 or 40 houses in Kula by Pozega in Croatia that were supposed to be swapped. I got into my car, I took some of these addresses and I didn't like those properties that I went to. It so happened that I went to Jaksic and I accidently bumped into this man, and I asked him whether he wanted to swap and he said yes. So we reached some kind of an agreement and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you. You said that people had arrived, these were Serbian refugees who wanted to swap houses. You said that there were also ads for house swaps, then you told us that on your own volition, you decided to try to look for a house, and you ended up in Jaksic. So before talking about the exchange with the owner in Jaksic, I would like to know why you wanted to leave? What was the motivation behind that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, what were the reasons. My uncle had been killed, threats were coming in every day. These groups of five, six or seven men would break into the yard and they were saying that I had to leave. These threats were being issued every day. A man could not go on living in a normal way. You could not work all day and get proper rest at night if there was this kind of pressure every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One small detail. You just said that there were groups of men who came every day to threaten you. Were these groups made up of Serbian refugees who had left Croatia or were they Sibincic's people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there were Serb refugees there, but there were also armed groups there too. I don't know who they belonged to, but they always had pistols, some of them even had hand grenades and some even wore camouflage military uniforms. So the psychological pressure was even greater that way. They would unbutton their shirts and they would show their belts with hand grenades and pistols.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you decided to leave, and you drove to Jaksic. Who did you meet there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as we drove through Jaksic, we stopped precisely this man with whom I swapped houses. He was on a tractor, and we asked whether he knew of someone who wanted to swap his house and he said that he did. We went to his house, we had a look at everything, and after that, his two sons-in-law and two daughters came to see our house because they had been living in Belgrade, and that is how the agreement on the swap was made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was his name, this person that you swapped houses with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we redact the name of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely right. Mr. Registrar, we need to redact the name that is on line 17 of page 82, because that might help identify our witness. There's a 30-minute lag anyway, so this mistake will be fixed easily. Now, could you please describe his house. How many rooms, did he have a tractor, was there any farmland? Describe his house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His house also had three rooms, a kitchen, a bathroom, a toilet, all of that. It was similar to our house except that the building style was a bit different. Also, perhaps some of the smaller buildings were a bit smaller, however, you can never have an exchange that is absolutely equal. However, their tractor was smaller, it had fewer accessories, and therefore, it was agreed that at that time they would pay us 2.000 Deutschemark for the machinery because theirs were less valuable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you agreed and on top of the house exchange, he also gave you 2.000 Deutschemark. Was there a contract for this agreement, and if so, where was it signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We signed a contract, of course, about exchange of real estate and machinery. The contract was signed in the municipal building in Pozega. It was drafted by a lawyer, and so it was signed in Pozega and then again it was signed also in Ruma.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was registered with a Tribunal in Ruma. As part of this exchange, were you a loser or a winner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when you get to the bottom line, the only thing where I was a loser was with land. But if you have to choose between safety, a safe life, it is better to opt for safety, for being alive, then for some land, because if you're dead, you can't really do anything with land anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a theory put forward by the associates of Mr. Seselj, the Defence case, and I shall tell you what this is about and ask you what your feelings are, that is the role of the Bench to confront the theory put forward by the Prosecution and by the Defence. Now, this is what the Defence submits. The Croats expelled the Serbs who lived in Croatia, and after that, there were two waves of Serbs who went to Serbia, who used to live in Croatia. One first wave including 200.000 Serbs around the year 1992, and another wave of 200.000 Serbs in 1995. All in all, 400.000 Serbs left Croatia to come and settle in Serbia. The Defence theory runs as follows: All these Serbs who left Croatia were forced to leave, were driven out. Some of them were mistreated and so on. I will not go into the details of all this. On the other hand, Croats, like you, living in your community and other communities, other villages, left for Croatia, and these Croats amounted to 1.000 or so people. We don't have an exact figure for the time being, but supposedly, 1.000 or so Croats went back to Croatia to go live there. So this is my first question: Do you agree upon the figures with me? A lot of Serbs arrived from Croatia and a number of Croats left for Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't keep statistical data so I don't know the figures for people who moved from one side to the other and vice-versa, but I'm sure that more Serbs came from Croatia into Serbia and Vojvodina than Croats who left the Serbian Vojvodina to go to Croatia, because there were more Serbs living in Croatia than were Croats living in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another theory put forward by the Defence during cross-examination a while ago, runs as follows: The Croats who, like you, left Croatia met up with Serbs to exchange their houses, and given that the Serbs were intimidated and victimized, they seized this opportunity since the Serbs had to leave Croatia and exchange their flats with people like you who had come to see them. And you said that you yourself went to Croatia and went to see the person whom you were going to exchange your house with. Is this true or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that I went to Croatia to look at the house that I was to swap, but it is also true that Serbs could come to our village to look at the houses that they would swap. It is not true that we, on both sides, could not see the houses and the property that we would be exchanging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another argument put forward by the Defence which we are submitting to scrutiny as follows: Among those Croats that left Hrtkovci, most of them were not wealthy people or people of an average income who left because they had small houses and small plots of land whereas the wealthy Croats who had large houses and a lot of land stayed. In other words, the underprivileged Croats left for Croatia whereas the wealthy Croatians stayed. What do you think of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, there are some rich Croats who remained because they were able to pay Sibincic protection money, so that he would leave them alone. And I know that there are rich Croats who went to Croatia, and you can check that if you look at the houses in Hrtkovci that Croats had left behind, and then look at the houses that they got in the exchange in Croatia. It is easy to say I left a bad house and got a better one. It all depends on whether houses are in villages or in towns or in big cities, because the value of a house here in the centre of The Hague is different from the value of a house on the outskirts of The Hague, just to give you an example. But there is a village of Ciglenik or Porec near Pozega, even if houses that were there were better than the ones that the Croats left in Hrtkovci, the problem is location. Those villages are really in the back of beyond, so even if it's a big house it's worth nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... among the farmers, since you were a farmer, were you a poor farmer, did you have an average income or were you wealthy, in what category would you have been put at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was medium income.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You'd be an average income earner. You said something which we haven't heard so far; nothing escapes me. As soon as I hear something new, I put the question to the witness directly to ask for more detailed information. You said that wealthy Croats had given money to Sibincic to be able to stay and left alone. Was Sibincic racketeering people and telling them, I shall protect you, but you need to give me some money and then you won't have any problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, something like that. That's what I heard some Croats say. I shouldn't really give you their names. But it is not true that only Croats moved out, there were Hungarians who were quite well off who moved to Croatia. They didn't want to pay the protection money to Sibincic and they had to move out. My uncle also moved to Croatia, to give you another example. He was also well off. He had all kinds of farming machinery, a lot of land, so it was not the rule for just middle class and the lower income people moved out into Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You quoted your uncle as an example. What was the surface area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, he had over 15 hectares of his own land. He had all the accessories for the tractor and for the harvesting of sugar beets, because our area was well known for sugar beet, so he left all of that and went to Croatia. There was also our village doctor. He had 15 or 20 acres of land and he farmed the land, yet he left it behind and he went to Croatia and he is unemployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, as far as you are concerned, a number of Croats left for Croatia and they weren't the winners in this exchange, they were the losers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, yes. We were the losers. First of all, land in Srem is much better. It yields much more than the land in this part of Slavonia around Pozega, Nasice, Slatina, Bijelova [phoen], for instance. The land there is much poorer than in Srem, in our parts in Srem. And if Mr. Seselj or somebody else, if you don't believe me when I say that, you can find experts who are going to test the land.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber has enough time, it can go and visit the area to see how much land there is, but for the time being we don't have time to go there. We shall see. Let me now talk about something which is in your statement. You said that your uncle -- well, that something happened to your uncle. Could you tell us what this is, but do not give us his name. Let's move into private session. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session now, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, you said that you saw people looting houses. It seems that you witnessed this with your own eyes. Can you tell us exactly what you saw as far as looting of these houses is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three houses down the road from my house, a group of people broke into my neighbour's house, and this neighbour of mine was in Croatia looking for a house for the exchange. His brother-in-law was there looking after the house and this group of maybe 15 or 20 people simply threw him out of the house, and this house was then occupied by a Serb from Croatia. In the meantime, my neighbour was able to exchange his house with a Serb from Rijeka, and when this man came to Hrtkovci, he couldn't get into the house. He had to allow the other man who was already in the house to take everything out, all the things that he wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One witness told us that the Serbs who had been driven out of Croatia were very discontent and they were blaming the government for not doing anything, and we were told that a lot of them were armed and walking around armed. Did you see this with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I saw armed people moving around because they came into my yard and they threatened me at gunpoint. They had pistols, some of them even had automatic weapons. But as they went around, they were usually protected by the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are saying that the police was protecting them. My last question, a great number of Serbs come to your village and they are looking for houses because they need to sleep somewhere. It seems that a lot of them are armed and they burst into houses in the way you described, but what was the state doing? What was the police doing, standing nearby, powerless, because everyone is overtaken by the situation? Why did the JNA not come to establish or re-establish law and order? What kind of explanation can you give us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an explanation. The police did nothing, as I indicated in my statement, until I spoke with the president of the Ruma municipality after my uncle's murder. She said I have to come to Hrtkovci and deal with the situation but I can't do it with the police in Hrtkovci, I have to come with the special forces. When she came to the village a couple of weeks later with the special forces, then law and order were re-established. Nobody broke into houses, we Croats started moving out in an orderly fashion. Roadblocks were set up at the entry and exit roads in the village so that some control was established over who got in and out and then there was a lull. It was it is my opinion that until that time, the police was commanded by somebody else, and I don't know whether the president of the Ruma municipality was given approval by Milosevic or somebody else at the top to calm the situation in Hrtkovci down a little bit or not, but my opinion is that she was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the Bench put questions, new information surfaces. You have just mentioned something which we have never heard before. You were saying that the president of the municipality in Ruma had been advised of the crime and you said that this person did something about it. Special police forces purportedly came and re-established law and order. Roadblocks were set up along the roads, when did this actually happen, what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] July, that's when peace was restored. So in 1992, before the month of May, after the month of May, June, that's when law and order is re-established, before that it was unruly, is that how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, something like that. The unrest followed Mr. Seselj's visit to the village, and then once the special police entered the village, then this unrest was lesser. There were still some provocations, but less attacks on the houses. People were not evicted from their houses anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's something interesting in what you said. These special forces arrive in July, and law and order is re-established, but after July, Croats decided to leave. They could have just stayed. Croats left after July, did they?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to redact line 21, page 92, I need to do all things at once. Please make sure that this is done. They left after that, but they didn't have to leave since law and order was back again. Why did they leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what kind of a life is it if you have to be under police guard all the time? We were not used to that. We were used to moving around freely. So they were guarding us in the village, but out in the fields, what about that? They were destroying our crops. You go into the field and you see somebody else harvesting your crop, watermelons, potatoes, and somebody can just kill you there in the fields just like that. They had weapons. We didn't have weapons. We didn't have anything to defend ourselves with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When exactly did you exchange your house, on what date? I didn't ask you that question. On what date did you exchange your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 18th of August, as far as I can remember. That's when I moved to Croatia. That was the date of the final move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on the 18th of August, you left when order was restored; is that right? Last question. Every time I say it's a last question, but I always put a last question after your answers. When you went to Croatia after 1992, 1993, 1994, you worked, then you gave the OTP a statement in 2002. At some point, did the Croatian intelligence services or the Croatian office of the prosecutor or Croatian police officers, did they come and visit you in your house or on your farm to ask you whether you were prepared to testify for this Tribunal? Were you contacted in such a manner or did you not see anyone save for the representatives of the OTP who was represented by Mr. Paolo Pastore-Stocchi, whom we all know. Did you see anybody else apart from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That day when I gave the statement, a representative of the Croatian police in plain clothes came to my house and he asked me if I wanted to give the statement and I said I wanted to, and then I went to actually provide the statement. But that was only on that day that I gave the statement to Mr. Stocchi, that's when this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Croatian police officer didn't tell you that you should say such and such and not such and such? Nobody tried to influence you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody exerted any influence. I came home from work, I didn't even have lunch. This gentleman came and told me you should come to such and such a place, they are waiting for you there. So I took my own car, I didn't go in his car. I took my own car. I waited there for maybe an hour or two hours until it was my turn to give a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm turning to members of the Bench to see if they have any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were not there when Mr. Seselj delivered his speech, but had you heard about security and did you know who was in charge of these security measure, the local police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I really don't recall that too well, about the security at that rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll turn to my colleague. No questions. I'm turning to the Prosecution, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MS. PRASAD
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into the private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, let's move to private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session, let me say that the witness's written statement has been tendered and -- under P654 [as interpreted] under seal. Mr. Witness, I would like to thank you -- First, Mr. Seselj, you do confirm that you not want to ask any questions for cross-examination purposes, right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not going conduct a cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to thank you on behalf of my colleagues and myself. Thank you, sir, for come coming to testify for the Prosecution. I wish you all the best for your return home. Before you leave this courtroom, we need to drop the blinds. I think you can leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Mr. Seselj, let me discuss the schedule for next week. The Trial Chamber has handed out a decision that was filed today. It might take some time to have it translated into your own language and you might not have it on time. This has to do with Mrs. Ewa Tabeau, expert witness for the Prosecution scheduled for Tuesday and Friday [as interpreted]. The Trial Chamber decided that Mrs. Tabeau, the expert witness, will come on those days. She will be examined in chief by the Prosecution for 30 minutes, using her report as a basis for this examination-in-chief. After which, Mr. Seselj, you will be given two hours, I repeat, two hours to cross-examine this expert witness. After this, if need be, the OTP will be entitled to ask additional questions and will be granted one hour to do so. Of course, the Judges are also entitled to ask questions but no time will be set aside for the Judges in all this time. I want to make a correction, I said it was Tuesday and Friday -- Tuesday and Wednesday and the transcript reads Tuesday and Friday. So I want to repeat the days for Ewa Tabeau are Tuesday and Wednesday. For Thursday we have another witness. This is what we've scheduled for Mrs. Tabeau. After all this the Trial Chamber -- after having heard both parties on the questions, the Trial Chamber will rule as to whether this expert report will be admitted or not. I wanted to tell you all this because I'm sure that you will not get our decision in your own language in time because it is several pages long and I think you needed to be informed of this. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I should wait a minute for the blinds to go up. Mr. President, Mr. President, I'm surprised that you decided in advance to give the Prosecution one hour for re-examination. Of course, I'm not opposed to it at all, but I want my rights to be protected as well. First of all, I come from a legal system in which the Defence always has the last word in relation to the Prosecutor. So whatever the Prosecutor says in court, the Defence is always entitled to respond. Here the Prosecutor gets an entire hour for re-examination whereas their examination-in-chief is two times less, half an hour. In other systems, the Defence usually gets more time to cross-examine an expert witness because there's usually an accompanying expert report. Now, if the Prosecutor is going to re-examine twice as long as the examination-in-chief is supposed to take, then there are various dangers looming there of the Prosecutor raising questions that they did not bring up during the direct examination, or things that I did not bring up in cross-examination, or they have the possibility to analyse even further what I brought up during my cross-examination. Therefore, I ask that if some new questions are raised, you give me time for my additional questions too. I believe that that would be fair. That was the first thing that I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, let me answer right away. The Trial Chamber could very well have decided to admit the report directly, and only to allow you for cross-examination. Some Trial Chambers proceed in such a manner. However, in order to guarantee your rights, we decided to grant the Prosecution half an hour to ask a few questions on the report. I believe that that is sufficient. After that, you will have two hours, which is a lot of time, for your cross-examination, and as we said in our decision, if need be, Prosecution -- the Prosecution is entitled to redirect, to ask additional questions. That's in the rules. We decided that given the magnitude of which you may explore in your cross-examination, the Prosecution might need an hour for redirect. If you need, of course, to reply on a few things, you know, you will be allowed to do so. Mrs. Tabeau is a demographer. She will be talking about statistics, population breakdown, a lot of tables, and so forth and so on. The Prosecutor might have some additional questions and maybe not, but if they do you will have the floor after them also.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well I have two more things to raise. First of all, as far as Ewa Tabeau is concerned, you've given me two hours. I believe that it may happen, I cannot say in advance, that I may need somewhat more time. I would like to draw your attention to the fact that I've saved up quite a bit of time during cross-examinations of the last few witnesses. Next week, Ewa Tabeau is the only witness that was envisaged. There's going to be another 92 ter witness, that's going to be very short, so we have three days at our disposal. Please bear that in mind, if I need more time, more than two hours, please grant me that time. I usually don't ask for that, but I would ask in the case of an expert, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll keep this in mind, no problem.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third thing that I wanted to raise, today I got a new witness schedule for October, November, and December from the OTP. This schedule was changed to an enormous degree compared to the one I had earlier on. There are three problems on the basis of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you are going to mention the name of protected witness, it would be best to move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I'm just going to refer to numbers. First of all, there are eight witnesses there who are Defence witnesses. As the Trial Chamber, you haven't ruled yet with regard to my voluminous request pertaining to the protection of Defence witnesses. Secondly, yet again I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. We handed out a decision, I believe that it is been translated. At the moment I'm looking at my legal officer and she is nodding, so we have handed out a decision regarding this. Unfortunately, there is always, you know, a time lag between the handing down of the decision and the translation of such decision. We work extremely quickly, as you know. We try to work as quickly as possible so you are not left hanging, but the decision has been handed down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, on the basis of this, I conclude that the OTP informs me that you have rejected my request, otherwise they wouldn't put (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is best not to mention the pseudonyms and their numbers because it might be possible to identify the persons with these numbers. We will redact all these numbers. But I can confirm that on the schedule there are people who you claimed as Defence witnesses, but that the Prosecution wants to call as their witnesses, and the procedure to call them is under way at the moment. Now, whether they will come or not, we will see, and if they do not come, the Trial Chamber will take the necessary steps. But as of now, they are on the schedule and we wanted to inform you of this because you need to know who is scheduled until December 12th.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
